Desperately
DES-per-it-ly
adv.
From Latin desperare (to despair, to give up hope), through Old French desperat; appearing once in the Authorized Version, intensifying Jeremiah's indictment of the deceitfulness of the human heart.

Biblical Definition

The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?

Desperately appears once in the Authorized Version, in one of Jeremiah's most quoted single verses, intensifying wicked to the point of naming a condition beyond ordinary description or repair. The word does not describe an occasional lapse but a settled, thoroughgoing corruption — desperately here carries the older sense of beyond hope, incurable by any human remedy, not the modern sense of urgent effort. Jeremiah pairs this with deceitful above all things, so that the verse names two linked problems at once: the heart's corruption is not only severe but also hidden from the very person whose heart it is, which is why the question who can know it? follows immediately rather than any confident diagnosis. The verse stands near the head of Reformed anthropology's doctrine of total depravity, precisely because it refuses the comforting assumption that self-examination alone can uncover the heart's true state. The verse that follows in Jeremiah supplies the only adequate answer: I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins — what is desperately wicked and hidden from the man himself is not hidden from God, who alone can both diagnose and heal it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from DESPERATE: beyond hope; irrecoverable; extremely bad; here as the adverb, desperately, intensifying the wickedness of the human heart in Jeremiah's classic diagnosis.

expand to see more

DESPERATE, adj. Without hope; beyond hope of recovery or cure.

DESPERATE, adj. Extremely bad; in the last stage of ruin or corruption.

DESPERATELY, the adverb, to a degree beyond hope or remedy.

In Jeremiah 17:9 the word intensifies 'wicked,' naming a corruption beyond self-diagnosis.

The following verse answers the question the verse raises: only the LORD searches the heart.

Key Scripture

Jer 17:9 — "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?"

Modern Corruption

A therapeutic reading softens 'desperately wicked' into ordinary human imperfection or a call to greater self-awareness, missing that the verse's whole point is that the heart's corruption cannot be adequately diagnosed by the very self-examination such readings recommend.

expand to see more

A self-help gloss on this verse can turn it into encouragement toward deeper introspection — know your heart better and you will master its deceit — precisely inverting Jeremiah's point. The verse does not counsel more careful self-examination; it declares self-examination inadequate to the task, since the heart deceitful above all things deceives the examiner as readily as anyone else.

The historic Reformed reading of this verse is not a pessimistic invention but the text's own conclusion, confirmed in the next verse's turn to God as the only competent searcher of hearts. The principle to recover is that desperately wicked names a condition requiring external diagnosis and external remedy — the LORD's own searching and trying — rather than a project the sinner can complete by looking harder within himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Desperately occurs once, intensifying Jeremiah's classic diagnosis of the deceitful heart, a verse foundational to the doctrine of total depravity and answered immediately by the LORD's own claim to search the heart.

expand to see more

Desperately in Jeremiah 17:9 intensifies 'wicked' to name a corruption beyond ordinary description.

The verse pairs this with 'deceitful above all things,' hiding the corruption from the man himself.

The rhetorical question 'who can know it?' expects the answer: not the man himself.

Jeremiah 17:10 answers directly: 'I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins.'

The verse is foundational to the Reformed doctrine of total depravity.

Usage

"The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked — corruption beyond self-diagnosis."

"Who can know it? — a question answered not by introspection but by the LORD's own searching."

"I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins — the remedy the verse itself supplies."
